findings.title: Tied CryptoProviders are chosen non-deterministically
findings.body: detectProvider no longer throws when ServiceLoader finds more than one CryptoProvider. It sorts by order() descending and returns the first entry. DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, and FIPS1402Provider all return 200, so any two of them tie, and ServiceLoader order is classpath-dependent. The loser is only mentioned in a debug log. Previously this misconfiguration aborted startup. Now a FIPS deployment that also has the non-FIPS provider can keep running with DefaultCryptoProvider even though FIPS1402Provider's constructor has already inserted BCFIPS at JCA position 1 and rewritten ssl.KeyManagerFactory.algorithm / ssl.TrustManagerFactory.algorithm. The process then mixes a non-FIPS CryptoProvider with FIPS JCA settings, or the reverse. When several providers share the highest order, startup should still fail.

findings.title: order() breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations
findings.body: order() was added as an abstract method with no default on the public CryptoProvider interface in keycloak-common. Implementations compiled against the previous interface will not compile, and at runtime ServiceLoader detection calls order() and throws AbstractMethodError, so CryptoIntegration.init fails and the server does not start. A default such as default int order() { return 0; } would keep older providers loadable and sort them below the in-tree providers (200) and AuthzClientCryptoProvider (100).

findings.title: getBouncyCastleProvider returns the JDK keystore provider
findings.body: getBouncyCastleProvider() is documented to return the BouncyCastle or BCFIPS provider. This implementation returns KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider(), which is the platform keystore provider (typically SUN), not BouncyCastle. WildFlyElytronProvider returns null when BC is absent so callers can take a non-BC path. A non-null SUN provider fails those null checks and is then passed to Signature.getInstance or Cipher.getInstance. SUN does not provide SHA256withECDSA (that is SunEC) or BC algorithms such as AES/CBC/PKCS7Padding, so provider-pinned operations throw NoSuchAlgorithmException or use the wrong implementation. For a standalone authz-client this class is the selected CryptoProvider, so return null or throw instead of handing back the keystore provider.

findings.title: AuthzClient.create freezes the JVM crypto provider
findings.body: AuthzClient.create(Configuration) calls CryptoIntegration.init(AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader()), and init() keeps the first provider it detects forever. ServiceLoader on the authz-client classloader does not see CryptoProvider services registered only in a child deployment or server classloader. Those order-200 providers are skipped, AuthzClientCryptoProvider (order 100) is installed, and a later CryptoIntegration.init from the server is a no-op. The rest of the JVM then uses a provider that throws UnsupportedOperationException from getSignature, getPemUtils, cipher, certificate, and truststore methods. Creating a client must not permanently install this stub from the library classloader; a later init that can see a higher-order provider has to be able to replace it.

findings.title: ECDSA integer conversion silently truncates
findings.body: integerToBytes, used by asn1derToConcatenatedRS, copies the low-order qLength bytes whenever BigInteger.toByteArray() is longer than the coordinate size. It does not require the discarded prefix to be a single 0x00 sign octet, and it does not reject a negative INTEGER. An oversized or negative DER integer therefore becomes a different R or S instead of failing the conversion with IOException. Signature verification then runs against a value that is not the encoded integer, so malformed ECDSA input is mishandled rather than rejected. Throw unless the encoding is at most qLength+1 bytes and any extra leading byte is 0x00.

findings.title: ECDSA test only checks a self-roundtrip on P-256
findings.body: The only new coverage of the ASN.1 ECDSA conversion generates one key with KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair(), which is the provider default curve (P-256 on standard JDKs), then runs ES256, ES384, and ES512 with that key. The sole assertion is that decoding the encoder's output matches the intermediate R||S. Signature.verify is never called, and the result is never compared with Java's original DER. A decoder/encoder pair that ignores the real R and S and inverts each other would pass. ES384 and ES512 also never see 48-byte or 66-byte coordinates, so the sign-octet padding path at those widths is untested. Each algorithm needs a key on secp256r1, secp384r1, or secp521r1, and the DER produced from the concatenated form must verify with Signature.verify.
